Yes

This is a bounded, measurable experiment tied directly to product value. It preserves task-force governance, board accountability, role boundaries, and full polling for mid-window amendments. The one-cycle acknowledgement target addresses the demonstrated delivery delay without over-specifying implementation. Three cards provide evidence before keep, revise, or drop at retro; counter-metrics expose bypasses and policy churn. It changes no standing rule and leaves open FAIL behavior intact.

CITE: the product owner's decisions reach the team within a cycle

Support-it

The design is minimal. It adds no seat, file type, card or checker, and it fits D183 because the inbox is not filed as issues. The experiment's metric is evidence only, so it can't produce a false-positive block.

Two tunes:
- Define "cycle" and "arrival" concretely. For example, count arrival from the timestamp of the first read, and acknowledge by the next boundary. Without that, "within one cycle" can't be checked.
- The inbox sits outside the repo, so enforcement rests on the facilitator's self-report. Copy each acknowledgement line into the card or closure record, so the retro can verify it from committed files.

C4 is sound. It matches the polled-amendment precedent in D187.

CITE: product-owner decisions to the team within one cycle instead of hours

No

The external mutable file has no committed arrival evidence, cycle identifier, or automated check, so a late, fabricated, or incomplete acknowledgement can still satisfy the metric. C1–C4 name obligations but provide no red-first detector for missed boundary reads, issue misuse, absent records, or quiet mid-window edits. The cited voice and in-progress files are also absent from committed HEAD. I would vote yes if each rule had a failing fixture and a committed checker reconciling immutable arrival/boundary timestamps, acknowledgement destinations, issue creation, and amendment polls.

CITE: each at the boundary where it was read

Yes

C4 helps me most: a rule change mid-window arrives as a polled amendment, not a quiet edit under my feet. I can comply without gaming it, because the acknowledgement is the facilitator's act, not mine.

One watch item: "cycle" in C2 isn't defined, and the metric's count (3 of 3, but "four" for the retro input) is loose. Tighten both at the next retro.

No

The channel, arrival time, acknowledgement, and UTC timestamp all live outside the repository, so neither C1/C2 compliance nor the metric can be verified from git. The cited retro voices and in-progress record are also absent from committed HEAD. This leaves a decisive loophole: entries can be omitted, backdated, or acknowledged after the cycle while the committed retro still claims 100%. I would vote yes if each inbox arrival and acknowledgement were append-only committed evidence with card/cycle identifiers and timestamps, while sensitive content could remain external.

CITE: every entry is acknowledged inside the cycle it arrived in.

Support-it

The experiment is cheap, reversible and time-boxed. It also has counter-metrics and a named keep, revise or drop decision at the card 3 retro, so the decision will rest on evidence.

Two weaknesses to tune:
- The metric measures the facilitator's compliance with their own rule, with no independent check. The product owner should confirm receipt, or the entry timestamps should be auditable.
- The baseline is anecdotal ("hours"). Record the arrival-to-delivery time for the earlier incident so "within one cycle" can be compared with something.

Seats look sufficient: the Decider signs off, and the product owner is the channel's user.

CITE: gets product-owner decisions to the team within one cycle
